attempts.why: well-formed-looking first attempt: swap both cases in one call, omitting both anchors (per guidance, omitting top_test_case means top of page and omitting bottom_test_case means bottom of page — with only 2 cases in the folder this should mean 'the whole page')
attempts.error_verbatim: {"errors":"Atleast one of top_test_case or bottom_test_case must be present"}
attempts.note: Neither top_test_case nor bottom_test_case is marked required in the declared contract (both are plain optional body fields), but the API rejects omitting both. This is an UNDECLARED requiredness constraint: at least one anchor is mandatory in practice, contradicting the schema. It also means a folder's entire case list can never be reordered in one call by specifying only the new sequence — an anchor into the existing list is always required, which is awkward on a 2-case folder where the only possible anchor IS one of the two cases being reordered.

attempts.why: retry with one anchor supplied: move TC-54504 (1985217) to sit above TC-54503 (1985216), swapping their order
attempts.note: Succeeded. Write response's own test_cases array came back in the new order [1985217, 1985216]. Verified independently by list_folder_test_cases read-back immediately after (see probe below) — read-back matched the write response exactly.

attempts.why: destructive-shaped test: anchor against a case from a DIFFERENT folder (TC-54502 / 1985215, native to folder 765817) while sending only one native case in test_cases and omitting the folder's other native case (1985217) entirely from the request
attempts.error_verbatim: {"errors":"Atleast one of top or bottom test case should be active and should have a valid order value"}
attempts.note: Different error message than attempt 1's (both are 400 under the same bare {errors: <string>} envelope). Confirms the API validates that an anchor must belong to (be 'active' / have an order value in) the target folder — a cross-folder anchor is cleanly rejected, not silently honored. No reparenting risk from anchors.

attempts.why: destructive-shaped test: include the FOREIGN case (1985215, native to folder 765817) directly inside test_cases (the moved-block list itself), alongside a valid native case, anchored on the folder's other valid native case
attempts.note: Succeeded, HTTP 200 {success:true}. The foreign id (1985215) does NOT appear anywhere in the response's test_cases array (still exactly 2 rows: 1985216, 1985217) — it was silently dropped from the move list rather than rejecting the call or reparenting the case. Verified by reading BOTH folders back independently: folder 765883 still holds exactly its 2 native cases in the new order, and folder 765817 (the foreign case's home) still holds its original 2 cases unchanged — no reparenting occurred. This silent-drop is undeclared behavior (nothing in the contract says invalid/foreign ids in `test_cases` are filtered rather than erroring).

attempts.why: destructive-shaped test: include a NONEXISTENT case id (999999999) inside test_cases alongside one valid id, anchored on the folder's other valid case
attempts.note: Succeeded, HTTP 200 {success:true}. The nonexistent id was silently dropped; the move proceeded using only the valid id (1985217), landing it above 1985216. This is the 'silent 200 half-success' bucket the task flagged as one of several distinct nonexistent-id behaviors seen across this product's routes (others give clean 400, bare 404 {success:false}, 404 {error:...} with no success key, or 502) — reorder_test_cases_by_folder's answer is: silently drop the bad id and honor the rest, 200 all the way, with nothing in the response indicating anything was dropped.

attempts.note: Succeeded. Folder restored to its original order [TC-54503 (1985216), TC-54504 (1985217)], confirmed by independent read-back.

notes:
IS ORDER OBSERVABLE AT ALL? Yes, but only IMPLICITLY. No test-case row — on this write's own response, on list_folder_test_cases, or on list_test_cases — carries any position/order/sequence field. The only field named 'order' anywhere in any of these schemas is test_case_steps[].order, which is the order of STEPS inside one case, unrelated to folder position. Manual folder order is visible only as array sequence on a folder-scoped, unsorted read (list_folder_test_cases with no sort_by). Verdict is therefore NOT UNVERIFIED — array-sequence is a real, working observable, and I independently reconfirmed it via read-back (never trusting the write response alone) across every attempt in this probe: the write response's order matched the subsequent list_folder_test_cases read every single time.

DOES AN EXPLICIT SORT OVERRIDE MANUAL ORDER, AND CAN THE CALLER STILL SEE IT AFTERWARDS? Tested directly: with the folder in manual order [TC-54503 (1985216), TC-54504 (1985217)] (createcases, then bulkcase — alphabetically 'b' < 'c', so alphabetical and manual order intentionally disagreed), calling list_folder_test_cases with sort_by=name-ASC&required[fields]=name returned [TC-54504 (1985217), TC-54503 (1985216)] — the ALPHABETICAL order, not the manual one. Answer: yes, an explicit sort_by fully overrides and masks manual order on this read, and there is no separate field anywhere in the row that discloses the underlying manual position once a sort is applied — the only way to see manual order is to omit sort_by entirely. Combined with the already-known finding that list_test_cases sorts by priority NAME alphabetically rather than by severity, and that sort_by+required[fields] combinations 422 unless the sorted column is included, this product's folder/case readers treat 'order' as a display concern with no persistent, sort-independent way to surface manual position to a caller who wants both a sort AND the manual sequence in the same call.

PARTIAL-LIST BEHAVIOUR (the destructive-shaped question). Sent test_cases containing only ONE of the folder's two cases in the successful probe call itself (attempt n=2: test_cases=[1985217] only, with bottom_test_case='1985216' supplying the second case purely as an anchor, not as part of the moved list) and again in attempt n=6. In both cases the OMITTED case (referenced only as an anchor, never inside test_cases) kept its position correctly and was never removed, appended elsewhere, or altered beyond the expected shift from the other case moving past it — confirmed by read-back showing cases_count unchanged at 2 and both TC-54503/TC-54504 present throughout. Because this folder holds only 2 cases and the API requires at least one anchor (see attempt n=1), it was not possible to omit the second case from the request ENTIRELY (with zero reference, not even as anchor) — the folder's small size forces every reorder call to name both cases in some role. Within that constraint, this route does NOT show edit_test_run.test_case_ids' destructive full-replace behavior: unmentioned-as-a-mover cases are left alone, not detached. This is a genuinely different (safer) shape from that precedent.

DIFFERENT-FOLDER CASE ID (reparenting risk). Tested two ways: (1) as the anchor (attempt n=3) — cleanly rejected, 400, 'must be active and have a valid order value', no side effect; (2) inside the test_cases move-list itself alongside a valid native case (attempt n=4) — succeeded 200, but the foreign id was silently DROPPED from the moved block; verified by reading back BOTH folders that the foreign case (TC-54502 / 1985215) never left folder 765817 and never appeared in folder 765883. No reparenting defect found on this capability — unlike some other routes in this product, a foreign-folder id here is either rejected (as anchor) or silently ignored (inside the move list), never actioned.

NONEXISTENT CASE ID. Sent 999999999 inside test_cases alongside a valid id (attempt n=5): 200 {success:true}, nonexistent id silently dropped, valid id moved as if it had been sent alone. This is the 'silent 200 half-success' bucket among the four/five distinct nonexistent-id behaviors now on record across this product's write routes (others: clean 400, bare 404 {success:false}, 404 {error:...} with no success key, 502) — reorder_test_cases_by_folder adds this fifth, no-error-at-all variant to that catalogue, and nothing in the response signals that anything was filtered.

CASES_COUNT ACCURACY. Read via list_folder_contents at the very start of the probe (cases_count:2, total_cases_count:2) and again independently mid-probe after the nonexistent-id write (cases_count:2, total_cases_count:2, sub_folders_count:0) — both accurate, matching the two prior confirmations on record and settling the third the task asked for: cases_count stayed correct across writes in this probe too.

FOLDER-MOVE CONCURRENCY. Read the folder's own record (list_folder_contents) immediately before the very first write: parent_id was null (folder sits at project root, not nested, despite its 'subfolder' name — presumably a prior probe already relocated it, or it was created that way). Read again after the write sequence: parent_id still null. No concurrent move was observed landing during this session; the reorder writes and the folder's own parent/location were confirmed orthogonal, as the task predicted.

OVERALL: functionality is real and works correctly — manual reorder actually persists, is independently verifiable via read-back, does not delete or silently reparent cases, and correctly rejects invalid anchors. Verdict is DRIFT rather than PASS because of concrete contract mismatches: (1) top_test_case/bottom_test_case are declared fully optional but at least one is actually mandatory; (2) the declared 200 schema promises a top-level `info` object that never actually appears; (3) the declared error envelope ({success:false, error:{code,message,details}}) never matches the real one ({errors:"<string>"}); (4) the write response includes ~10 undeclared per-row fields beyond the declared schema.
